project.name: PharmaShield GCC
project.tagline: Choosing medicine suppliers on evidence, not on price alone
project.customer: a UAE hospital group purchasing organisation (GPO)

how_it_works.title: Collect
how_it_works.text: Pull public data: who may sell the drug, FDA inspections, recalls, shortages, warning letters, World Bank logistics scores, and 10,000 past medicine shipments.

how_it_works.title: Identify the factory
how_it_works.text: Find the factory that really makes each product from its official drug label. Several brand names turn out to be one factory.

how_it_works.title: Score five risks
how_it_works.text: Cost, late delivery, billing oddities, compliance and route exposure. Each runs from 0 (best) to 1 (worst).

how_it_works.title: Rank and split
how_it_works.text: Rank the suppliers with the board's priorities, then split the monthly order across independent factories.

how_it_works.title: A human approves
how_it_works.text: Nothing is ordered until a category manager signs off. Every approval is logged and tamper-checked.

criteria.plain: How expensive one vial is, compared with the other suppliers.
criteria.method: Official US Medicare price list (one price for all generics). Freight to the UAE has no data and is left out.
criteria.method_synthetic: Synthetic view: official US price + real insurance + synthetic air freight (R3, R5). Mark = how much dearer than the cheapest, capped at 1.

criteria.plain: The chance that a shipment arrives late.
criteria.method: An XGBoost model that learned from 7,771 real medicine shipments (up to 2013) and was tested on 2,545 later ones. The top 3 reasons are shown for each supplier.
criteria.method_synthetic: Synthetic view: the same trained model, given each supplier's synthetic shipping terms and delivery record (R1-R4, R10, R11).

criteria.plain: How often the supplier's invoices look unusual.
criteria.method: An Isolation Forest flags the oddest 5% of invoice lines. A supplier with no invoice history of its own scores 0 (the plan's rule).
criteria.method_synthetic: Synthetic view: the Isolation Forest runs on synthetic invoices of the 5 established suppliers (R7); new suppliers keep 0.

criteria.plain: How clean the factory's record with the US drug regulator is.
criteria.method: FDA inspections and warning letters for the factory that makes the product, plus the seller's injectable recalls.
criteria.method_synthetic: Synthetic view: the same FDA record plus 20% from each supplier's synthetic contract (R6).

criteria.plain: How exposed the supply route is to a Hormuz or Gulf-airspace disruption.
criteria.method: One evidence-based exposure share for every origin, adjusted by the origin country's World Bank logistics score.
criteria.method_synthetic: Synthetic view: a synthetic air-route share per factory (R9), adjusted by the same World Bank logistics score.

real.label: Real data
real.plain: Measured, with a cited public source.

standin.label: Stand-in
standin.plain: Real data about something close, used because the exact data is not public. Labelled as such.

nodata.label: No data
nodata.plain: Nothing exists, so every supplier gets the same neutral value and it cannot change the ranking.

judgement.label: Team setting
judgement.plain: A stated choice by the plan or the team, visible and adjustable.

synthetic.label: Synthetic
synthetic.plain: Invented within an approved industry range, synthetic view only. Its range and source are listed on this page.

evidence_ledger.input: Who is allowed to sell the drug
evidence_ledger.note: 18 labelers; 11 sell finished vials and are ranked. 7 sell only raw powder and are excluded.

evidence_ledger.input: Which factory makes each product, and where
evidence_ledger.source: Official drug labels (DailyMed) and the FDA establishment registry
evidence_ledger.note: Known for 10 of 11 suppliers. One label does not say, so that supplier gets neutral values.

evidence_ledger.source: CMS Medicare Part B payment limits, October 2026
evidence_ledger.note: A US reimbursement price, not a UAE tender price. One price covers all generics; the branded product has its own, far higher price.
Left out of the cost, so it is the same for every supplier.

synthetic.source: Ranges R3 and R5 (vial weight x air-freight rate by origin)
synthetic.note: $0.30-0.60 a vial, added to the official price.

evidence_ledger.note: Not guessed. Each supplier's score is averaged over real past shipments from its factory's country.

synthetic.note: Each supplier gets its own shipping mode (air), delivery terms and shipment size; the delivery model scores that profile.

evidence_ledger.note: None of the 11 has 5 or more past shipments of its own, so all are treated as new suppliers. This is about delivery history with buyers, not about whether they make carboplatin: that comes from the FDA product list and the drug labels.

synthetic.source: Ranges R10 and R11, using real US market share
synthetic.note: The 5 suppliers with at least 9% US market share get 6-24 past deliveries to this buyer at 80-95% on time; the other 6 stay new.

evidence_ledger.note: Set to 0 for every supplier, the plan's rule for new suppliers. Because it is the same for all, it has no effect: removing its 5% weight leaves every score, rank and vial unchanged.

synthetic.note: Synthetic invoices for the 5 established suppliers with 1-4% errors; the billing model flags the odd lines. New suppliers keep the plan's 0.

evidence_ledger.note: Counted only for the factory that makes the product. Other plants of the same company are shown as a note, never scored.

evidence_ledger.source: openFDA drug enforcement reports, last 5 years
evidence_ledger.note: Serious recalls of injectable products by the company on the box. Companies with more products tend to have more recalls.
A sample, not every letter. 'No letter' means none in our sample.

evidence_ledger.note: Not scored. The contract reader is shown as a demo only.

evidence_ledger.source: UAE port volumes (Jebel Ali vs Khor Fakkan)
evidence_ledger.note: One share, 0.85, for every origin. No evidence supports different shares by country.
The only part of route exposure that differs between suppliers.

evidence_ledger.note: Sterility and data integrity count most.

limits: The late-delivery model learned from HIV-medicine shipments to other regions between 2006 and 2015. It captures how shipping behaves in general, not oncology supply to the Gulf.

In the real data no supplier has its own delivery or invoice history, so all 11 are treated as new suppliers and the billing mark is the same (0) for all, with no effect on the ranking. The synthetic view shows how the system behaves once such history exists.
Only 50 FDA warning letters were read. A supplier with no letter here may still have one.
Prices are US reimbursement prices. Real tender quotes would replace them in a live system.
Several marks are equal for many suppliers because invented differences were removed. The ranking leans mostly on the FDA record, the delivery model and the country logistics score.
This is a prototype for a course project. It is not procurement advice.
The synthetic view fills gaps with invented values. They are plausible, not true: use it to see how the system behaves with fuller data, not to choose a real supplier.

governance.title: A human decides
governance.text: The system recommends. A category manager approves, overrides or rejects, and the decision is logged.

governance.title: Explainable
governance.text: Every supplier shows why it scored as it did: the top 3 delivery-risk reasons and what its compliance mark is made of.

governance.title: Fair to suppliers
governance.text: A supplier is scored on its own factory and its own history, never on a country name alone or on a parent company's record.

governance.title: Privacy (UAE PDPL)
governance.text: No personal data feeds the scores. The approval log stores initials or a staff ID only.

governance.title: AI disclosure
governance.text: The code and this site were produced with Claude and reviewed by the team. The contract extraction is AI-generated; it is not scored in the real view, and is scored (marked synthetic) in the synthetic view.

plan_differences.plan: Rank all 18 authorised labelers (§3).
plan_differences.here: 18 confirmed; 11 ranked.
plan_differences.why: 7 of the 18 (including Cipla and Hetero) list only the raw ingredient and cannot supply hospital vials (plan §4.1: only makers authorised for the target product).

plan_differences.plan: Blend the board's weights 50/50 with data-driven entropy weights (§4.2).
plan_differences.here: The board's weights decide; entropy is a slider from 0% to 50%.
plan_differences.why: With 11 suppliers and many ties, two standard entropy formulas gave opposite weights and the ranking swung. The plan itself lists the entropy slider as optional (cut order item 3).

plan_differences.plan: Cost from 2026 tender quotes plus origin freight markups (§4.3).
plan_differences.here: One official US price for all generics, Avyxa's own price; freight left out.
plan_differences.synthetic: The same US price plus synthetic air freight by origin (R3, R5).
plan_differences.why: No public tender quotes or UAE freight costs exist. Real tender quotes would replace the stand-in in a live pilot.

plan_differences.plan: Late-delivery risk from each maker's shipping mode, terms and freight (§3.1).
plan_differences.here: Averaged over real past shipments from each factory's country.
plan_differences.synthetic: Each supplier's own synthetic shipping profile and delivery record (R1-R4, R10, R11).
plan_differences.why: Shipping details for UAE orders are not public, so the real view guesses no single value.

plan_differences.plan: Route exposure from each origin's Hormuz and Gulf-air share (§4.3).
plan_differences.here: One evidence-based share, 0.85, for every origin.
plan_differences.synthetic: A synthetic air-route share per factory, 0.90-1.00 (R9).
plan_differences.why: UAE port volumes support one share; no public evidence gives different shares by country. The World Bank logistics score still differs by country.

plan_differences.plan: Compliance includes an AI reading of each supplier's contract (§4.3).
plan_differences.here: The contract term is 0 for everyone; the contract reader is a demo.
plan_differences.synthetic: The 11 synthetic contracts are scored and count for 20% of compliance (R6).
plan_differences.why: The contracts were invented for testing, so scoring them in the real view would rank real companies on fiction.

plan_differences.plan: Plant capacity is a hard limit in the order split (§4.4).
plan_differences.here: Capacity never limits the split; the share caps do.
plan_differences.synthetic: Synthetic capacity of 1,500-8,000 vials a month per factory (R8).
plan_differences.why: Factory capacity is not public.

plan_differences.plan: Share caps per supplier (§4.4).
plan_differences.here: Share caps per factory.
plan_differences.why: Several brand names are made in the same factory (Teyro makes Apotex, Natco and Teyro; Gland makes BPI and Gland), so capping names would not spread risk.

plan_differences.plan: Order quantities x ≥ 0 (§4.4).
plan_differences.here: Whole vials.
plan_differences.why: A vial cannot be split; solving in fractions left orders of 0.1 vial.

plan_differences.plan: A 70/20/10 example split (§1.3, §2, Q&A 4).
plan_differences.here: 30/30/30/10 across four factories.
plan_differences.synthetic: 37/33/15/15 across four factories, and Crisis mode changes it.
plan_differences.why: The plan's caps (70% established, 15% new) are upper limits, not targets. With no supplier history every factory is capped at 30%; with synthetic history the split prefers the higher-ranked new suppliers up to their 15% cap.

plan_differences.plan: Probation trial share: a mandatory 5-10% (§3.1, §4.2, Q&A 5) versus 0 or at least 5%, capped at 15% (§4.4).
plan_differences.here: The order-split rules (§4.4) are followed: a new supplier gets 0, or between 5% and its cap if it is chosen (decision L2).
plan_differences.why: The plan contradicts itself; §4.4 is the formula the solver needs, and forcing every new supplier in would override the ranking.

plan_differences.plan: A 4-tab Streamlit cockpit with a live AI contract reader (§5.2 step 9).
plan_differences.here: The Streamlit cockpit (4 tabs plus a data-pipeline tab) and a 9-page website; the contract reading is cached.
plan_differences.why: The website lets anyone explore without installing Python. A cached contract reading is the plan's own fallback (cut order item 2).

plan_differences.plan: Scenario stress-testing (Q7).
plan_differences.here: Natural-disaster stress test: any factory or every factory in India offline.
plan_differences.why: Shows what dual sourcing protects against, using only real factory locations; no invented probabilities.

plan_differences.plan: Cost mark scaled from the cheapest (0) to the dearest (1) supplier (§4.3).
plan_differences.here: The plan's formula.
plan_differences.synthetic: How much more expensive than the cheapest, capped at 1.
plan_differences.why: With synthetic freight, a 30-cent difference on a $28 vial would otherwise fill the whole 0-to-1 scale. On the real data both formulas give exactly the same marks.

plan_differences.plan: Real or scenario data for every input (§3).
plan_differences.here: Evidence only: a cited source or 'no data'.
plan_differences.synthetic: Gaps filled with values from approved industry ranges, each marked.
plan_differences.why: Asked for by the course professor. Every synthetic value is marked, its range and source are listed, and no model is trained on it.

plan_differences.plan: An active FDA shortage adds a penalty to compliance (§3.2 dataset table).
plan_differences.here: Shortages are shown as alerts and badges, not scored.
plan_differences.why: The plan's own compliance formula (§4.3) has no shortage term, so the formula was followed; a shortage tells the buyer to confirm supply, it does not measure quality.

plan_differences.plan: World Bank political stability (WGI) as a route input (§3.2 dataset table).
plan_differences.here: Fetched and shown in the Streamlit profile, not scored.
plan_differences.why: The plan's route formula (§4.3) uses only the logistics score (LPI).

plan_differences.plan: Monthly model retraining and a 3-6 month probation until the buyer's own delivery history builds up (Layer 5, §3.1).
plan_differences.here: Not built: described as part of the 90-day pilot.
plan_differences.synthetic: The synthetic delivery record shows what that history would change.
plan_differences.why: Both need the buyer's own deliveries over time, which a prototype cannot have.

plan_differences.plan: Tier 1 needs the highest safety stock (§4.2).
plan_differences.here: Not modelled.
plan_differences.why: The plan gives no number or rule for safety stock; the split covers one month's demand.

plan_differences.plan: USAID GHSC-PSM data as an out-of-time check for the delivery model (§3.2, optional).
plan_differences.here: Not used.
plan_differences.why: The plan's own cut order drops it first; the model is checked on 2014-2015 shipments it never saw.

plan_differences.plan: A live openFDA shortage feed (Q7).
plan_differences.here: Website: snapshot of 15 Nov 2026 plus a live FDA check button. Streamlit: live pull.
plan_differences.why: A static website cannot call the FDA on every page load without slowing every reader; the live button does it on request.

plan_differences.plan: A risk weight lambda that sets how much the split pays for safety versus price (§4.4).
plan_differences.here: Fixed at 1.0; there is no dial on the dashboard.
plan_differences.why: All ten generic suppliers cost the same, so any positive setting gave the same split (only 0 differed); a dial that changes nothing was removed. It would matter once suppliers quote different prices.

glossary.meaning: In pharma: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient, the raw drug powder. In software: Application Programming Interface, a way for our code to fetch data from a website (for example "the openFDA API").
In pharma: the official printed information for a drug (on DailyMed). In AI: the correct answer attached to a training example (for example "this shipment was late").
The buyer collects from the factory gate. The buyer arranges all transport.
The seller hands the goods to the buyer's transport company.
The seller pays freight and insurance to the destination.
The sea-freight version of the same idea.
The seller delivers to the destination. The buyer handles import taxes.
The older name for DAP.
The seller does everything, including import taxes. It arrives at your door.
Not an Incoterm. In the SCMS data it means "shipped from the aid agency's own regional warehouse".
The cost of transporting the goods.
The cost of insuring the goods during transport.

The total cost to get one vial to you: price + freight + insurance. C1 is based on it. In the real view freight to the UAE has no data, so it is left out; the synthetic view adds synthetic air freight (ranges R3, R5).
Freight cost divided by goods value. A $4,000 freight bill on $5 of goods is suspicious.
Air, sea (ocean) or truck.
A whole aircraft hired for one shipment.
The route goods travel, for example India to Dubai by sea.
The narrow sea passage into the Gulf. Ships to Dubai's main port must pass through it.
The sky over the Gulf region. Flights into the UAE can be rerouted or suspended when it closes.
A narrow route with no easy alternative.
UAE ports. Jebel Ali is inside Hormuz. The other two are outside, so they are safer.
A storage area where imported goods can sit before import taxes are paid.
An extra shipping fee charged when a route becomes dangerous.
Keeping a drug refrigerated for the whole journey.
A World Bank score from 1 to 5 for how good a country's shipping and customs are.
A World Bank score for how politically stable a country is.
A chemotherapy (cancer) drug. It is our demo product.
The drug substance itself (carboplatin), regardless of brand or maker.
Cancer medicine.
HIV medicines. Our old shipment data is mostly these.
HIV rapid test kits. The second-largest product group in the old shipment data.
A drug given by needle, and the small glass bottle it comes in.
A vial that holds several doses.
The physical form of a drug: tablet, injection, cream.
How much drug is in each unit. Ours is 10 mg per mL.
Completely germ-free. This is critical for injections, so sterility failures are the most serious.
Germ-free manufacturing, and the practice run a factory does to prove it works.
Tiny particles, or bacterial residue, found in a product. Common reasons for recalls.
A copy of a drug sold by many companies once the patent has expired.
The raw active ingredient before it becomes a finished vial. 7 of our 18 companies sell only this, so we do not rank them.
The ready-to-use vial. Only the 11 companies that sell this are ranked.
One specific product, for us "Carboplatin Injection 10 mg/mL".
The US government's drug regulator.
The FDA's free public database.
The US ID number for a drug product. The NDC Directory lists who is allowed to sell what.
The company whose name is on the box. It is not always the company that makes the drug (Apotex's carboplatin is made by Teyro Labs).
A factory that makes a drug for another company to sell under its own name.
A company that only re-boxes someone else's product. Excluded from our list.
Legal permission to sell a drug.
A factory or lab registered with the FDA for a specific job (manufacture, testing, labelling).
The website holding official drug labels, and the label file format.
Two types of US approval. ANDA is for a generic copy. 505(b)(2) is for a modified version, such as Avyxa's branded Kyxata, which is why it is expensive.
Avyxa's brand name for its carboplatin.
"Current good manufacturing practice", the factory quality rules.
The FDA visits a factory to check it.
Inspection results: all fine / minor issues / serious problems. OAI is the red flag.
The FDA's ID number for one factory.
The list of problems inspectors hand over at the end of a visit.
A formal public FDA letter saying a factory has serious problems.
An FDA order that stops a factory's products at the US border.
Whether factory records are honest and complete (not deleted or backdated).
Proof that the manufacturing process gives the same result every time.
The factory's internal quality-control team.
The US rulebook for drug factories. Warning letters cite sections of it.
The equivalent rulebook for factories that make raw ingredients (APIs).
FDA inspections of clinical-trial sites, not factories. We exclude them.
A product pulled from the market. Class I is the most dangerous and Class III the least.
The FDA's list of drugs in short supply.
The World Health Organization's list of must-have drugs.
The US Medicare price list, its "average sales price", and the billing codes (carboplatin is J9045). We use these as our price stand-in.
The price an insurer pays for a drug. A public stand-in for a real supplier quote.

The old US aid programme's record of about 10,000 medicine shipments (2006–2015). It is our "teacher" data.
The US aid agency that ran it.
A newer version of the same kind of data. It is optional and we skipped it.
A stand-in used when the real data is secret or missing.
A number the team chose because no real one exists. It must be labelled as such.
Made up for testing. Our 11 supplier contracts are synthetic.

A second version of the results, switched on in the website's side bar, where every input with no public evidence is filled with a value invented within an industry range. Each such value is marked "synthetic". The real view never uses them.
The lowest and highest value a synthetic number may take, with the industry report or real data it is based on (file `synthetic/reference/synthetic_ranges.csv`).
A supplier with at least 5 past deliveries of its own. The plan lets its factory take up to 70% of the order; a new supplier is capped at a trial share.
The list of manufacturers we score (18 in total, 11 rankable).
The final table: one row per manufacturer, with all five marks.
A series of steps that turn raw data into the final table.
Fetching data and loading it into our system.
Our code asking a website for today's data.
A saved copy of what a website returned, so the run can be repeated without the internet.
A frozen copy of the data at one moment.
A simple table file that opens in Excel.
A text format for structured data.
The agreed list of columns in a table. "Locked" means nobody changes it.
Squash numbers onto a 0-to-1 scale so they can be compared.
One way to normalise: the lowest becomes 0 and the highest becomes 1. It can stretch tiny gaps.
Fill in a missing value with a reasonable guess.
The middle value when the numbers are sorted.
The value that 90% of the numbers fall below.
A value far from normal.
Set bad rows aside with a reason, not silently delete them.
Remove repeated rows.
Force text into a number or date, turning unreadable values into blanks.
How far into the past we count. Ours is 5 years for inspections and recalls.
Working out that "Hospira Inc" and "HOSPIRA, INC., a Pfizer Company" are the same company.
A tool that scores how similar two names are (0–100).
Another name for a company, or its owner (Eugia is owned by Aurobindo).
Personal details such as names, emails and phone numbers, and blacking them out.
A fingerprint of a file. If the file changes, the fingerprint changes.
The shared project folder on GitHub, saving a set of changes, and uploading them.
A list of files that are deliberately not uploaded.
A private install of Python tools for one project.
A document that mixes code and its results, run from top to bottom.
The tool that turns our Python code into a web page (the cockpit).
A small automatic check that a piece of code does what it should.
A program that learns patterns from past examples to make predictions.
One input the model looks at (country, shipping mode and so on).
The thing the model tries to predict. Ours is "was the shipment late?"
Teach on one part of the data, then examine on another part the model never saw.
A third slice used for choosing settings, so the test stays untouched.
The exam uses later years than the teaching, which is like predicting the future.
The model accidentally sees the answers while learning. A form of cheating.
The model memorises the teaching data and then does badly on new data.
Splitting the data into parts and taking turns, so every example is scored by a model that never saw it.
A setting of the model, and trying several to pick the best.
A fixed starting number so the result is identical every run.
A popular prediction method built from many small decision trees. It produces our C2.
A simple, classic prediction method.
The simple method you must beat to justify the fancy one.
The model's answer as a chance between 0 and 1.
Using a trained model to score new cases.
Scoring a supplier from its characteristics (country, mode) instead of its own history.
The cut-off above which we call something "late".
An overall score for a predictor. 0.5 is coin-flipping and 1.0 is perfect. Ours is 0.80.
Of the truly late shipments, the share we caught (92%).
Of the ones we flagged, the share that really were late (20%).
Flagged as late but arrived on time.
Not flagged but arrived late.
Single numbers that combine recall and precision. F2 counts recall more.
A 2×2 table of right and wrong predictions.
Only 11% of shipments are late, so the model would ignore them. This setting makes it pay more attention to late ones.
How often something happens overall (11% late).
A factory's past late rate, used as an input.
Pulling a rate based on very few shipments towards the overall average.
The new cases differ from the teaching data (oncology vials vs HIV pills).
A method that explains why a model gave a score: "these 3 things pushed it up".
Which inputs the model relies on most overall.
Being able to show a human why the model said what it said.
A method that finds unusual rows. It produces our C3.
A setting telling it to flag the oddest 5%.
Learning without correct answers. Isolation Forest is unsupervised.
Getting computers to read text.
Turning text into numbers by counting the important words.
A model that sorts things into categories.
Answers produced by a rule instead of a human. Ours come from which regulations a letter cites.
A large AI language model, such as Claude.
Asking an LLM to do a task with no training examples.
Teaching the model again on newer data. The plan says monthly.
The five marks: cost, late delivery, billing oddities, compliance, route risk. Each runs from 0 (best) to 1 (worst).
Multi-criteria decision-making: choosing when several things matter at once.
The table of suppliers (rows) against the five marks (columns).
How much each mark counts towards the final rank. They add up to 1.
A method that turns the bosses' opinions ("delivery matters more than cost") into weights.
Comparing the marks two at a time. This is how AHP collects opinions.
A check that those opinions do not contradict each other. It must be below 0.10.
Weights worked out from the data itself: a mark that varies more counts more.
The plan's mix: half AHP (opinion) plus half entropy (data). This prototype uses the board's AHP weights by default, with entropy on a slider (it proved unstable on 11 suppliers).
The formula that combines the five marks into one rank, by closeness to an ideal supplier.
An imaginary supplier with the best (or worst) value on every mark.
TOPSIS's result, from 0 to 1. Higher is better.
Maths that finds the best order split under rules, and the Python tool that does it.
A number the maths is free to choose. Ours is how many vials each supplier gets.
What the maths tries to minimise. Ours is cost plus a penalty for risky suppliers.
A rule the split must obey, such as "max 70% to one supplier".
Whether any split exists that obeys all the rules.
A safety valve. Ours is the emergency spot buy, so the maths always has an answer.
A huge made-up cost on the spot buy, so it is used only as a last resort.

The weight the order split puts on risk compared with cost. Fixed at 1.0 (the plan's default); there is no dial on the dashboard, because all generics cost the same and changing it made no difference.
A yes-or-no choice inside the maths, such as "is this supplier used at all?"
The maximum share one supplier may get.

The plan's example split: main supplier, backup, trial supplier. It needs a supplier with its own delivery record. In the real view all suppliers are new, so the plan's rules cap each factory at 30% (split 30/30/30/10); in the synthetic view 5 suppliers are established and the split is 37/33/15/15.
Three preset weight settings. Crisis shifts weight from cost to route risk.
In Crisis mode, route risk is multiplied by 1.5.
Asking "what if this bad thing happens?" and re-running the numbers. Here: a natural disaster takes factories offline and the order split re-solves.
Changing one input to see how much the answer moves.
A person must approve every recommendation.
A permanent record of who approved what and when.
Cannot be edited afterwards.
The UAE's personal-data privacy law (Federal Decree-Law 45 of 2021).
Collect only the personal data you need, and use it only for the stated reason.
The UAE's 2024 principles for AI: transparency, human oversight, safety.
